title: (Draft) How many people drink and drive in El Paso, Texas?
text:
The Drunk Driving Iceberg


    In the year 2023, 752,449 people were arrested in the United States for driving under the influence.1 Although the number seems high, most people recognize DWI arrests only show the people who were caught—the tip of the iceberg. But just how much of the iceberg are we seeing? In total, how many people drink and drive? According to a national survey that same year, an estimated 15.6 million people admitted they drove under the influence.2 That means law enforcement agencies arrested about 4.8% of the offending population \((\frac{752,449}{15,600,000})\). Keep in mind, however, that the 15.6 million people who admitted to drunk driving are being counted only once (they were asked if they ever drank and drove, not how many times they did it during the year). Data from another national survey was able uncover the frequency of drunk driving, estimating the total number of drunk driving episodes in a year could be as high as 256 million.3 Using this number changes the proportion of people arrested for drunk driving, from 4.8% to less than one percent (0.29%). As a country, we know the iceberg is more of an ice mountain, and if we use DWI arrests as our measure of how big it is, we are severely underestimating the magnitude of the problem.     Turning now to the sun city, how does El Paso compare to these national estimates? How many El Pasoans drove drunk last year? How many times? Does the El Paso Police Department (EPPD) arrest 1, 4, or 8% of the people drunk driving in the city? The answer is no one knows. There has never been a city-wide effort to estimate the prevalence of drunk driving. That means the DWI arrests reported each week by the EPPD do not tell us just how much of the iceberg we are seeing. So what does DWI arrests tell us?     DWI arrests tell us more about the response to the problem than the problem itself. Changes in arrests reflect changes in enforcement activity, not the behavior we seek to change. Understanding the difference between DWI arrests and DWI behavior is important, as both are often confused with one another. To help explain the difference, take the following example: imagine a police department doubled their capacity for DWI arrests, increasing from 30 arrests in one week to 60 arrests the following week. Does this increase mean twice as many people were out drinking and driving? Not necessarily. In fact, DWI arrests is not the right information we need to answer this question because we have no idea how many people were actually out drinking and driving. What we do know in this example is the police department doubled their number of arrests in one week. The reasons for the increase might be explained by increased staffing or having patrol officers dedicating more time to traffic enforcement. In these cases, the offending population could have remained the same, while the enforcement activity by the department increased. On the other hand, if DWI arrests decreased from 60 to 45, again, it would not necessarily mean that less people were drunk driving. The decrease may be explained by the same reasons just mentioned.     By now, it should be clear that DWI behavior is the problem we are concerned with changing; we hope that fewer people will be driving intoxicated. But if DWI arrests is not a good measure of the problem, what is? Well, the survey mentioned earlier proposes one solution: just ask people if and how often they drive drunk. Now, you might be thinking, Hold on. I don’t remember being asked by someone if I drove drunk last year. Those survey numbers can’t be correct; how do they know? The answer might sound unusual: the researchers who administered the survey didn’t actually ask all 300 million Americans about drunk driving; they only asked about 70,000 (You read that right). The reason they do not survey everyone is because it’s expensive, and they don’t have to (it’s not because they’re lazy or stubborn). Researchers only need to use a little bit of statistics to figure out how many people in a population are needed to obtain what is called a representative sample: a group of people that reflect the population they are interested in studying. For example, when the presidential election approaches, many voters have already made up their mind on who to vote for. Rather than wait, some researcher companies, such as Gallup, will randomly select a group of people in a city or state and ask if they are voting for candidate A or candidate B. The results of their survey give a proportion (e.g., 46% said candidate A and 54% said candidate B). Using a simple statistical technique, the researchers calculate what is called a margin of error to show how certain or trustworthy their estimate is (looks something like this: \(\pm\) 2%). If their margin of error calculated to plus and minus 2 percent, then they would make the following statement: “We estimate that 44 to 48% of the population will vote for candidate A, and 52 to 56% of the population will vote for candidate B”. Pretty cool right?     Surveying 70,000 people is appropriate for estimating a variety of characteristics across an entire country. For a city of less than 700,000 people, however, far less people are needed. Although the minimum size of the sample is determined by several factors and requires careful planning, it is not unusual for researchers to find they only need 600 people to make useful estimations. For example, imagine a city-wide survey was conducted in El Paso, and the researchers asked participants about their drunk driving behavior, as well as other questions that could be useful. At the end of that effort, we can have the ability to say “This is our estimate of how many people admitted to DWI in the year 2026.” COnducting this kind of survey on a yearly basis gives us data over time, which tells us not only how big the problem is but how it is changing. Although conducting a survey would require a little bit of funding, the effort would give us, as a city, a more objective measure of the DWI problem. No longer would the DWI problem be a myth, but a studied problem that we know is either getting worse, staying the same, or hopefully getting better.

title: Open Criminology: El Paso, Texas
text:
One of the rights of passage for graduate students in a social science program is to produce original research, usually referred to as a capstone paper or thesis. The official purpose varies, but overall the capstone/thesis demonstrates a student’s expertise and knowledge on a specific topic. For instance, my thesis was a study on police officer’s perceptions of the public and organization.
Like other students, more time than I am willing to admit went into completing my research project. If you count the hours I spent designing the survey, jumping through bureaucratic hurdles to get approval, figuring out how to calculate a correlation, and revising my writing again, again, and again (), it took 15 days, 500 nights, and a concerning amount of caffeine (Do consider visiting a coffee shop on Sunday and purchasing a coffee for the sleep-deprived student you find staring at their laptop and rubbing their temples. Bonus points if you remind them their research is going to change the world, and they should stop scrolling on their phone and get back to work).
There are several carrots for getting that research project done. The obvious one is getting to wear a cool gown and hat and march around the Don Haskins Center like it’s your quincenera. Another important one is being able to click on a higher box for educational attainment in the online job application. Or, maybe the reward at the end is doing something no one else in your family had the opportunity to do. In that case, the reward is serving as a role model to your younger and older relatives (It’s never too late).
A less appreciated carrot, and what inspired Open Criminology El Paso, is getting other people to read your writing. Is it vain? Absolutely. As vain as a new parent who wants to show off their baby; writing a research paper is no less. Just like a new child, however, the magic eventually wanes, and you realize no one cares (for children, around age 8. I’m kidding. Everyone still cares about you). In all truth, most people will never read your thesis or capstone paper, even your own mother who promised. If you are lucky, your mom will read the introduction because you spent the most time reworking that section. If you don’t believe me, ask her what she thought about your findings (by the way, that’s what you look like in class when you didn’t do the assigned readings).
The fault is not with our moms, dads, grandmas, grandpas, or anyone we hoped would read our research. The fault is in the tradition of academic writing—researchers write for other researchers. While there is value in that, writing in coded language is at the expense of the community we hope our research will serve. In other words, the researcher who is double-checking your traffic stop analysis praises you for including an interaction term, while the city official who makes decisions is trying to figure out if anything you did was useful to them.
Open Criminology El Paso fills that gap. My hope for this website is to document local research being done in the city, and to translate the material into everyday language, or what I consider everyday language (it’s more fun my way).
For the community, this is a website that shows how our local talent is answering the questions that matter most to you.
For the city official, this is a website that shows you what we know, what we don’t know, and how to move forward in solving social problems. If you have a data analyst on your team, this website might teach them a useful trick or two.
For the researchers, this
For my parents, this is another chance to read something I wrote.
It’s not easy rewriting things, especially when you are trying to capture the nuance that only details
The research project in of itself, belongs to a tradition since the dawn of humanity. As old as the quest for fire. The graduate student engaged in a scientific reasoning. They answered a question that hadn’t been asked yet.
A getting this stack of papers published by the University or an academic journal. Like a new parent, a writer wants to show off their baby any chance they get.
Now, in the year 2026, I am pursuing a doctoral degree in criminology and criminal justice at Arizona State University. Through my journey in school, I learned about the value of research, particularly when it comes to solving social problems related to public safety.

title: About Open Criminology El Paso
text:
A right of passage for graduate students in a social science program is to produce original research, usually in the form of a capstone paper or thesis. The official purpose varies, but the idea is for the student to demonstrate expertise and knowledge on a specific topic. For instance, when I was a student at the University of Texas at El Paso, my thesis project was a study on how perceptions of negative media attention impacts police officers’ confidence in their authority.
Like other students, more time than I am willing to admit went into completing my research project. If you count the hours I spent designing the survey, jumping through bureaucratic hurdles to get approval, figuring out how to calculate a correlation, and revising my writing to make it comprehensible, it took 15 days, 500 nights, and a concerning amount of caffeine. (Do consider visiting your local coffee shop on Sunday and purchasing a drink for the sleep-deprived student you find staring at their laptop and rubbing their temples. Bonus points if you tell them their research is going to change the world, and they should stop looking at their phone and get back to work).
There are several carrots for getting that research project done. The obvious one is getting to wear a cool gown and march around the Don Haskins Center like it’s your quinceñera. Another important one is being able to click on a new box for educational attainment in the online job application. Or, the reward is doing something no one else in your family had the opportunity to do. In that case, you are a role model to your younger and older relatives (It’s never too late).
A less appreciated carrot, and what inspired Open Criminology El Paso, is getting other people to read your writing. Is it vain? Absolutely. As vain as a new parent who wants to show off their baby—writing a research paper is no less. Just like a new child, however, the magic eventually wanes, and you realize no one cares (for children, around age 8. I’m kidding. Everyone still cares about you). In all truth, most people will never read your thesis or capstone paper, even your own mother, who promised. If you are lucky, your mom will read the introduction section because you spent the most time making it enjoyable to read. If you don’t believe me, ask her what she thought about your findings (by the way, that’s what you look and sound like in class when you don’t do the assigned readings).
The fault is not with our moms, dads, grandmas, grandpas, or anyone we hoped would read our research. The fault is in the tradition of academic writing—researchers write for other researchers. While there is value in having someone familiar with The Code review your work, writing in The Code is at the expense of the community our research intends to serve. In other words, the researcher who is double-checking your traffic stop analysis praises you for including an interaction term, but the city official is trying to figure out if anything you did was useful to how they make decisions. And that’s assuming you distilled your 44 page document into a 30-second document. I can’t be any more clear: no one is reading your research papers.
Open Criminology El Paso seeks to fix that. My hope for this website is to document local research being done in the city, and to translate the material into everyday language, or what I consider everyday language (it’s more fun my way). I’ll do my best, but my best might not be good enough. I may resort to jargon or really goof in explaining something. Have pity on me, please. If something is not making sense, it’s not you, it’s me, so please consider sending me an email—you are my audience as much as my editor.
